To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

penetrating arteriole occlusion causes flow stasis in subsurface capillaries that is not relieved until a length scale consistent with the spatial density of penetrating arteriole branches is traversed.
penetrating arteriole occlusions cause a significant reduction in blood flow in subsurface capillaries, and that flow recovers within 350 mm from the site of occlusion.
penetrating arteriole occlusion results in severe ischemia in neocortical tissue, and the ischemia persists for minutes to tens of minutes in the absence of collateral blood flow.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spatial distribution and function of the penetrating arterioles that bridge the surface and subsurface microvascular beds of the cerebral cortex.
the role of the microvasculature in the delivery of oxygen to the brain.
how blood flow is regulated by the cerebral microvascular bed and how the regulation of flow is altered in the presence of disease or injury.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the penetrating arteriolar network is a major bottleneck in the delivery of blood in the event of penetrating arteriolar occlusion.
penetrating arteriole occlusion causes a severe and persistent reduction in flow in the subsurface microcirculation that surrounds the occlusion.
penetrating arteriole occlusion causes a bottleneck that is a major contributor to the severity of ischemia in neocortex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
penetrating arteriole occlusion is a severe insult that is likely to lead to tissue damage.
penetrating arteriole occlusion is a potent stimulus for ischemia, but it is also a potent stimulus for vasodilatation.
penetrating arteriole occlusions are associated with severe ischemia in a substantial fraction of the tissue they serve.
The main takeaway from our work is that

penetrating arteriole occlusion causes a dramatic reduction in blood flow to the underlying cortex and that this reduction in flow is maintained for a substantial distance downstream from the occlusive event.
penetrating arteriole occlusion causes a large and long-lasting decrease in the delivery of blood to the cortex, even when the occlusion is located far from the cortical surface.
a small number of penetrating arteriole occlusions may be sufficient to produce widespread ischemia in cortex.
